name: Follicular unit transplantation (FUT)

card.summary: Strip-harvest hair transplant: a scalp strip is removed and dissected into grafts, leaving a thin linear donor scar.
card.aka: FUT, strip harvesting, strip surgery, FUSS
card.note: Leaves a linear donor scar, which is the main reason many patients choose FUE instead.

quick.overview:
Follicular unit transplantation removes a thin strip of hair-bearing skin from the back of the scalp, which technicians dissect under microscopes into natural follicular units for implanting in balding areas.

It became the standard hair transplant approach in the 1990s and is often compared with follicular unit extraction (FUE), which avoids a strip incision.
quick.mechanism: Grafts from the donor zone retain resistance to pattern hair loss, so transplanted hairs are described as lasting. The strip method allows many grafts from a single session, with the wound closed by sutures.
quick.risks: The donor site retains a thin linear scar that is usually concealed by surrounding hair. Recovery includes stitches or staples and about two weeks of healing; shock loss and other graft-related effects are described.

lead: Follicular unit transplantation (FUT), also called strip harvesting, is a hair transplant technique used to restore hair density on a thinning or receding scalp. A strip of hair-bearing scalp is taken from the donor region at the back and sides of the head and divided under stereo-microscopes into naturally occurring follicular units, which are then implanted into balding areas.[1][2][3]

People use it to rebuild a hairline, fill in thinning crowns or restore eyebrow and beard hair, giving a fuller, younger frame to the face. A 2020 review describes hair transplant as a reliable procedure that can give natural, high-impact results with minimal downtime, and says it can be used for scalp, eyebrow, beard and body hair and for scarred areas.[4] Because grafts come from donor hair that resists pattern hair loss, transplanted hair is generally described as lasting.[1]

Wikipedia describes strip excision as replacing the older plug grafts, with microscopic dissection of strips developed in the late 1980s.[1] The method leaves a thin linear donor scar that is typically hidden by hair; a 2002 paper introducing follicular unit extraction (FUE) described scarring after strip excision as infrequent but concerning enough to motivate an alternative.[2]
infobox: Scalp, eyebrow, beard and scar-area hair[4]
About two weeks to suture removal[1]

paras: Wikipedia gives a typical strip size of about 1 to 1.5 cm by 15 to 30 cm, with assistants dissecting follicular units and the donor wound closed, sometimes with a trichophytic closure said to produce a finer scar.[1] Recovery is described as about two weeks, with removal of sutures unless they are dissolvable.[1]

A 2021 overview in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology describes modern hair restoration as based on follicular unit transplantation, in which follicular units are the exclusive grafts, and discusses how to identify good and poor candidates, since not all hair disorders are suitable for transplantation.[3] A 2020 review focuses on performing the strip technique specifically.[4]

Wikipedia describes Carlos Uebel and William Rassman popularising many small grafts in the 1980s, and B. L. Limmer using stereo-microscopes to split strips into micrografts in the late 1980s.[1] Walter Unger described the safe donor zone in 1994.[1] The 2020 review notes that earlier techniques such as hair plugs and scalp reductions left a negative public impression of hair restoration, which follicular unit techniques sought to move beyond.[4]

Wikipedia says FUE leaves scattered small scars rather than a linear scar, but involves longer surgery, higher cost and, according to some surgeons, a lower proportion of successful follicles.[1] Robotic systems for FUE harvesting have also been described.[5]

A 2021 German review describes hair transplantation as a procedure with low complication risk and great benefit for patients, while noting that no defined specialist standard exists and recommending thorough informed consent and consultation to avoid dissatisfaction.[6] A 2024 systematic review of 141 studies on androgenic alopecia treatments included hair transplantation among procedures that promote hair growth and highlighted multifaceted, individualised approaches.[7]

A randomised double-blind study in 10 patients compared three strip dissection techniques (tissue spreader, skin hooks and sharp scissors) by dividing each strip into three parts.[8] Reviews summarise FUT outcomes and complications more broadly.[3][4][6][7] The 2002 paper introducing FUE discusses FUT donor scarring as its motivation.[2]

timeline.event: Strip excision with microscopic dissection develops, replacing plug grafts.[1]
Walter Unger defines the safe donor zone.[1]
FUE introduced as an alternative to strip harvesting.[2]
Robotic FUE harvesting reviewed in Dermatologic Clinics.[5]

angle.text: FUT moves hair from the back of the scalp to the front or top, restoring a hairline and density that frame the face. Because many grafts come from a single strip, it is one way to cover large areas in a session.
